anti_generic_signature_read: Blind, asked what was memorable rather than generic: 'the red storm oval with its tan halo and, above all, the way the surrounding band buckles around it — that one detail does more characterisation than the stripes do. The out-of-phase waviness in the band edges is also a real choice; it keeps the ball from looking like a beach ball. The bare apricot polar caps against a busy equatorial belt is a correct and recognisable silhouette of decoration.' Against it, and recorded as given: the ball read as 'visibly low-poly', which the repair below removed, and the terrain cells as 'the weakest part'.
blind_action_read: 'View 1 is a single staged hero shot: one board fully populated with roughly fourteen pieces, plus the two empty trays hovering beside it. View 2 is a strip of three smaller renders of the same board at, apparently, three successive states — the left one is crowded, the middle one has about half as many pieces, the right one only four or five. Pieces disappear left to right, and the survivors are not in the same cells, so something is being removed and something is moving. That reads as a game progressing.'
blind_form_read: 'The large flat piece is a slab board with real thickness... Its top face is divided into a grid by thin raised ridges; the cells themselves are shallow recessed pans... so every square reads as a tray. Some of those recessed cells are filled with a raised terrain relief: brown/ochre pans covered in small pyramidal bumps (rubble or crater fields) that stand proud of the cell floor but stay below the grid ridges; one cell is flat black with three tall cyan cones standing well proud of the board; several cells are flat cyan with an etched sunburst/radial line pattern.' Pieces: 'a short cylindrical disc base (a squat puck with a rounded top edge and a small embossed glyph on its side wall), and a sphere sitting on top of it... the ball stands proud on a little pedestal. Bases come in two finishes, bright white and flat black.'
blind_held_read: Unprompted, before knowing what the object was: 'a tabletop board game, or the 3D model for one. There is a thick rectangular grey board divided into a grid of square cells... and a set of playing pieces: small spheres, each glued onto a round cylindrical token base like a chess piece or a miniature's base. Two separate flat grey trays with... scooped-out oval recesses each sit off to the side — component storage, or a supply/reserve rack. You'd stand the sphere-topped tokens on the board's cells and move them around; the terrain painted into the cells... suggests spaces that mean something different from each other.'
blind_relationship_read: 'Within the board, pieces sit one per cell, centred, never straddling grid lines, and they cluster loosely by base colour — white-based pieces occupy the near/left half, black-based pieces the far/right half. That looks deliberate: two sides, two colours, like opposing players. The terrain cells form a contiguous band of brown rubble across the board's middle and a separate cyan/black cluster at the far end, again deliberate rather than random scatter.'
blind_subjects_read: Named unprompted: 'These are planets. The pieces read as a solar system set' — Jupiter ('the large banded gold-and-cream ball with a red oval', very confident), Earth ('the small blue ball with green landmasses', very confident), Mars (confident), Saturn ('a pale yellow-cream banded ball with a flat ring through its equator', confident), 'Uranus and/or Neptune — a turquoise ball and a mid-blue ball', 'The Moon or Mercury', 'Venus — a plain cream/buff ball'. It named Jupiter correctly as the subject of all eight close-ups before being told anything.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, before being told any of it: 'Belt widths are visibly unequal (roughly 3:1 between narrowest and widest on the visible face), spacing is uneven, and there is no mirror symmetry about the middle.' On the sub-clause, primed and measuring pixels: 'the widest belt on the ball is the one immediately above the zone holding the spot -- about 57 px against 38-40 px for the three belts above it and 27 px for the one below... it is the largest dark mass on the globe and it is the band that carries the notch, so the spot and the belt read together.' MET. Re-checked on the final images after the interference repair and CONFIRMED MET: 'still about 57 px against 38-40 for the belts above it, and still the thing the eye takes after the spot'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 1. Six belts at Jupiter's real, unequal latitudes -- +38/+43, +24/+31, +7/+17, -7/-20, -27/-34, -40/-46, widths 5, 7, 10, 13, 7 and 6 degrees -- neither evenly spaced nor symmetric about the equator, with the South Equatorial Belt the widest and the one a viewer notices first after the spot.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'Over the middle it is overlaid with alternating bands in two colours: a saturated mustard/ochre gold, and an almost pure warm white.' Primed: 'Three distinct tones are unambiguously present: bare apricot globe at the poles, ochre belts, and a warm near-white zone filament... five zones, four full and one narrow sliver... The widest zone is now clearly the broad pale band across the middle, at about 65 px -- the widest single band of any kind on the ball.' MET. Measured separately at 46.5 luma levels from the globe and 78.3 from the belts. Re-checked on the final images and CONFIRMED MET.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 2. Five bright zones in a third, lighter filament between and beyond the belts -- Equatorial -7/+7 the widest, North Tropical +17/+24, South Tropical -27/-20, North Temperate +31/+38, South Temperate -40/-34 -- clearly lighter than both the globe and the belts.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'a solid deep red ellipse, clearly wider than tall (roughly three-to-two), lying in a pale/grey band in the lower third of the ball... It has a thin ochre/tan halo ring immediately around it, and the pale band it sits in deforms around it -- the boundary above it lifts into a small lens or teardrop shape, and the gold band above is locally pushed up, so the stripe is genuinely interrupted rather than merely overprinted.' The critic called the buckling 'the most convincing thing on the whole ball'. MET. Re-checked on the final images and CONFIRMED MET: 'the belt above still bending down into a lens-shaped hollow centred over it'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 3. The Great Red Spot as one oval 13 degrees of arc wide by 9 tall at latitude -22, wider than it is tall, inside the South Tropical Zone, with a darker collar just outside it and a hollow bitten out of the South Equatorial Belt above it so that belt bends around the spot.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'The band edges are not clean circles. Each boundary undulates in a slow wave... and different boundaries wave out of phase with each other, so bands pinch narrower in one place and swell wider in another.' Primed, on exclusivity: 'the four boundaries of the two broad middle belts wander; the thin upper belts... and the narrow belt below the spot run as clean arcs with no visible departure.' On amplitude the critic measured 5-6 degrees peak to trough, retracted its earlier 5-8 degree estimate and agreed with the built 2.50 degrees of amplitude. MET. Re-checked on the final images and CONFIRMED MET.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 4. A wavy boundary of two to three degrees on the two widest belts only -- South Equatorial and North Equatorial -- with the four narrower belts left as exact circles of latitude.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'Both the top and the bottom are plain: a smooth unbanded apricot cap covering roughly the top and bottom quarter of the ball, with no stripes at all.' Re-checked on the final images and CONFIRMED MET.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 5. The poles above +46 and below -46 left as bare globe, with no zone and no marking of any kind on them.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: 'I can see no oval, blob or light patch of any kind inside any belt, north or south, in any of the eight views. The only non-band feature anywhere on the ball is the red spot, and it is in a zone, not a belt.' MET. Re-checked on the final images and MET.

'No belt has any finger, streamer or hanging lobe projecting into the zone below it. The one downward excursion on the whole ball is the hollow above the spot, which requirement 3 calls for, and it is in the south.' MET. Re-checked on the final images and MET.

'The belt edges carry a slow, low-frequency wander and nothing else -- no small-scale ripple, no stipple, no fringing that I can attribute to the design.' The critic warned in round two that tessellation stair-stepping could be mistaken for edge texture; after the mesh repair it reported 'I can find no tessellation artefact anywhere in the eight close-ups'. critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Re-read on the final images: 'Views 1 and 2 still show what I recorded before, in every particular... the same fourteen-piece roster split white-base near and black-base far, the same two ten-recess trays... and the same three-state progression left to right', but recorded CANNOT TELL because the critic had only its own prose to compare against. Settled deterministically instead: measure/occurrence-geometry.md compares all 184 published occurrence labels against this run's 196 on solid count, exact volume and bounding box at 1e-4 mm3 and 1e-6 mm -- nothing outside jupiter_sol_* and jupiter_anti_* gained, lost or moved a solid.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 6g. Nothing else in the set changed: the other fourteen worlds, four panels, twelve belt tiles, six corona cells, two stars and two trays are exactly as they were.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: 'The silhouette is an exact circle in views 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10, including at the spot's longitude and along every belt edge. The globe reads as a true sphere.' MET. Re-checked on the final images and MET.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: On the final images: 'both globes carrying the same band sequence, the same spot in the same zone, the same collar and the same notch, so nothing contradicts a common map', but CANNOT TELL on the 3.13 degree lean, which the critic refused to call either way -- 'this has to be settled on geometry; images cannot do it, and I would not accept an image-based claim that it passes'. Settled on the geometry: every colour body of the Anti-Sol world matches its Sol twin in exact volume, the largest disagreement being 1.5e-5 mm3 on an 8,920 mm3 globe.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 6i. The two Jupiter pieces are exact mirrors of one another: the same map, with only the ownership cue inverted.

largest_risk: The reviewer's, and it is about the set around the corrected world rather than the world: 'The Jupiter piece reads finished. It is specific, it has a correct and legible hierarchy -- spot, then the belt bent around it, then the wide equatorial zone -- and it holds up under magnification from four angles without a seam, a facet or a stray tone. I would believe it came out of a catalogue. What it sits inside does not.' It named four things, none of them this correction's and all of them already disclosed in product.json: the black bases photograph as unlit voids under a flat-shaded renderer with no ground plane; three of the eight close-ups show the hemisphere the spot is not on; the trays read as floating for the same lighting reason; and the rank numeral sits on the disc wall, so it is legible in the hand and edge-on from a seated position. The last is the one worth a future run, and the reviewer said so: 'still the thing I would spend the next correction on'. This correction is forbidden to touch the numeral, which is a frozen dimension, so it is recorded rather than answered.
resolution:
PROTOCOL. Ten canonical images were copied into a scratch directory as view-1 ... view-10 so no file path could prime the critic: no Wish, no concept, no product name, and a rule that reading any other file voided the review. Its blind read was fixed before anything was revealed. Rounds two, three and four were primed and said so.

OUTCOME. Round one gave a real unprimed read: it named the object as a two-player planet board game, named Jupiter as the close-up subject, answered IRREGULAR to the regular-or-irregular question, and read the spot as part of the weather because the belt buckles around it. Round two, primed, raised three blockers, two of which became repairs. It refused to certify the renders as fresh; measured, it was right -- the chord tolerance was never binding, the mesher's 0.1 radian angular default was, and the project now passes 0.03 radians, taking one piece from 138,761 to 1,357,677 triangles. It reported the wrong belt reading widest; measured, the 12 degree camera put its own sub-point at planet latitude +10 and foreshortened the South Equatorial Belt, so the per-world frames moved to 5 degrees. Neither repair touched the globe. Round three returned every open requirement MET and closed all three. Then the interference gate failed on the corrected world -- it reported the South Temperate Belt's whole 51.52 mm3 as a clash with the South Tropical Zone on one army and nothing on its mirror -- so the zones were re-cut to stop at each plain belt's exact latitude, every canonical image was regenerated, and round four re-examined all ten. It confirmed every requirement on the new files and found no regression and no blocking defect on the corrected piece. The words 'beach ball' appear once in the blind text, in 'it keeps the ball from looking like a beach ball' -- for what the piece avoids. Asked directly in every primed round the critic said it does not read as one; by round four, 'the phrase no longer comes to mind even as the thing it escapes'.
reviewer: One independent native critic, given the canonical images under neutral filenames and no Wish, concept or product name; its unprimed read was fixed before anything was revealed.
